questions.stem: You are doing a rectal examination on David, 75, in the ED for painless dark red rectal bleeding. He is in the left lateral position and the nurse is chaperoning. You have inspected the anus, asked him to strain, checked tone at rest and on squeeze, and swept the rectal wall and prostate. You now withdraw your finger. What is the next step?
options: Ask him to bear down again to check for a prolapsing internal haemorrhoid
Smear material from the glove onto an FOBT card to confirm the blood
Inspect the glove for blood, mucus and the colour of any stool
Remove your gloves, wash your hands and then tell him the findings
questions.why: Always look at the glove before you take it off. Fresh blood, melaena, mucus or pale stool tell you where the bleeding is coming from and what kind it is. Here it confirmed blood with no mass.
notes: Straining to look for prolapse belongs to inspection, before the finger goes in, and David has already done it.
FOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms. It adds nothing when the bleeding is visible, and a symptomatic patient needs colonoscopy whatever it shows.
This skips the glove inspection, and he should be cleaned and covered before you discuss the findings.

questions.stem: David, 75, is on day 2 after his colonoscopy and has had no further bleeding. HR 72, BP 118/74, no chest pain, no dyspnoea and no known cardiovascular disease. His repeat Hb is 96 g/L (baseline 141), MCV 89, ferritin 145 µg/L. What is the most appropriate plan for his haemoglobin?
options: No transfusion now; repeat FBC and transfuse only if Hb falls below 70 g/L
Transfuse 1 unit of red cells, as he is over 65 with an Hb below 100 g/L
Transfuse 2 units of red cells, as his Hb has fallen by more than 40 g/L
Give IV ferric carboxymaltose now, as his Hb has fallen below 100 g/L
questions.why: Australian Patient Blood Management guidance uses a restrictive threshold: transfuse at Hb below 70 g/L, or below 80 g/L with cardiovascular disease. A stable patient who is no longer bleeding and has Hb 96 g/L does not need red cells.
notes: Age over 65 is not an indication. Transfusing at Hb 70–100 g/L in a stable patient with no symptoms gives no benefit and carries risks such as fluid overload.
The size of the fall is not a transfusion trigger. The decision depends on the current Hb, whether bleeding continues and his haemodynamics.
His ferritin of 145 µg/L shows his iron stores are full, so IV iron is not indicated for an acute blood loss anaemia.

questions.stem: At 14:05, a few hours after passing a cupful of dark red blood, David, 75, has an Hb of 124 g/L against a baseline of 141 g/L. The sample is not haemolysed. Your registrar warns that this first result underestimates how much blood he has lost. Why does an early Hb underestimate an acute bleed?
options: The marrow releases reticulocytes within an hour, restoring red cell mass
Splenic contraction releases stored red cells into the circulation
Whole blood is lost, so Hb concentration falls only as fluid refills plasma
Plasma is lost faster than red cells from a bleeding vessel, concentrating blood
questions.why: An acute bleed removes red cells and plasma in proportion, so the Hb concentration hardly changes at first. It falls over 24–72 hours as interstitial fluid shifts in, the kidneys retain fluid and IV fluids dilute the blood.
notes: The marrow takes days to raise its output, and the reticulocyte response peaks at about a week. It does not restore red cell mass within hours.
In humans the spleen stores very few red cells, so splenic contraction does not explain a near-normal early Hb.
Bleeding loses whole blood, not plasma first. The delay comes from the time it takes for haemodilution to happen.

questions.stem: David's colonoscopy shows numerous sigmoid and descending colon diverticula and no other source of bleeding. You explain that diverticula bleed because of how closely they sit to the vessels in the colonic wall. Where do colonic diverticula typically form?
options: Through the taeniae coli, where the longitudinal muscle bundles are weakest
At the antimesenteric border, between the two antimesenteric taeniae
At the rectosigmoid junction, where the taeniae spread into a continuous coat
Where vasa recta pierce the circular muscle, between mesenteric and lateral taeniae
questions.why: Diverticula push out through weak points where the vasa recta pass through the circular muscle. That leaves the vessel stretched over the dome of the sac, where it can rupture and cause a sudden, painless, large bleed.
notes: The taeniae are thick bands of longitudinal muscle. Diverticula form in the gaps between them, not through them.
The area between the two antimesenteric taeniae has no penetrating vasa recta and is largely spared.
Where the taeniae merge into a continuous longitudinal coat at the rectum, the wall is stronger. This is why rectal diverticula are rare.
